item.description: Amnesty International has expressed concern over the continued denial of adequate healthcare, family visits and regular access to legal counsel to Pakistan's former Prime Minister Imran Khan and his ...
item.content:encoded:
Amnesty International raises alarm over Imran Khan, Bushra Bibi’s health, demands immediate medical care Amnesty International has expressed concern over the continued denial of adequate healthcare, family visits and regular access to legal counsel to Pakistan's former Prime Minister Imran Khan and his wife, Bushra Bibi, during their detention, describing the restrictions as a violation of Pakistan's international human rights obligations. ANI | Updated: 18-11-2026 14:55 IST | Created: 18-11-2026 14:55 IST

Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Amnesty International has expressed concern over the continued denial of adequate healthcare, family visits and regular access to legal counsel to Pakistan's former Prime Minister Imran Khan and his wife, Bushra Bibi, during their detention, describing the restrictions as a violation of Pakistan's international human rights obligations. In a post on X, Amnesty International said that Imran Khan has not been allowed to meet his family since December 2025, apart from two meetings with his sister in August 2026. The organisation further stated that he has not been permitted to speak to his sons over the telephone since March 2026. Highlighting concerns over his detention conditions, Amnesty International said that the 74-year-old former Pakistan PM has been held in solitary confinement and increasingly isolated from human contact, affecting his mental and physical health. It also pointed to reports of severe blood pressure issues and alleged that Pakistani authorities have denied him access to independent doctors despite an August Supreme Court order directing that he be taken to a private hospital. The organisation also raised concerns about the medical condition of Bushra Bibi, stating that she is suffering from an eye condition that could potentially lead to vision loss and has also been denied adequate medical treatment. Citing Pakistan's international human rights obligations, Amnesty International said that the treatment of Imran Khan and Bushra Bibi violates Article 10 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), to which Pakistan is a state party. The provision guarantees that every person deprived of their liberty must be treated with humanity and respect. The human rights organisation also highlighted concerns over the detention of Imran Khan's family members, alleging that his relatives have been targeted for advocating for his rights. According to the post, three of Khan's sisters were detained on September 20 and 21 under Section 3 of the Maintenance of Public Order, 1960, on broad and vague grounds linked to a planned march to Islamabad by Khan's political party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI). While two of his sisters were released last week, Amnesty International stated that Aleema Khan remains detained at Kot Lakhpat Prison in Lahore. Calling on Pakistani authorities to take immediate action, Amnesty International demanded adequate medical care for both Imran Khan and Bushra Bibi, along with the restoration of regular access to their family members and lawyers. The organisation further urged authorities to end what it described as the political persecution of Imran Khan's family, particularly his sisters, for speaking up for his rights. It specifically called for the immediate release of Aleema Khan and urged Pakistani authorities not to initiate further charges against family members for exercising their fundamental rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. (ANI)

item.title: The evolution of 007: Every James Bond actor over the years and the future of the franchise
item.description: For over six decades, James Bond has remained the gold standard of cinematic espionage. Since first ordering a vodka martini in 1962, the British Secret Service agent has constantly reinvented himself ...
item.content:encoded:
The evolution of 007: Every James Bond actor over the years and the future of the franchise For over six decades, James Bond has remained the gold standard of cinematic espionage. Since first ordering a vodka martini in 1962, the British Secret Service agent has constantly reinvented himself to match the mood of every era. From Cold War coolness to modern gritty realism, and now entering a bold new studio era, here is how 007 has evolved across the generations. ANI | Updated: 18-11-2026 14:34 IST | Created: 18-11-2026 14:34 IST

Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan, Daniel Craig, Robert Pattinson (Photo/Youtube/@JamesBond007). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

For over six decades, James Bond has remained the gold standard of cinematic espionage. Since first ordering a vodka martini in 1962, the British Secret Service agent has constantly reinvented himself to match the mood of every era. From Cold War coolness to modern gritty realism, and now entering a bold new studio era, here is how 007 has evolved across the generations. 1. Sean Connery: (1962-1967, 1971) (Image source: Reuters, Eon Productions) When Scottish actor Sean Connery stepped onto the screen in Dr. No, he didn't just play James Bond, he invented the cinematic spy. Effortlessly suave, ruthless when necessary, and armed with dry wit, Connery established the iconic tropes that still define the franchise today. He starred in six official Eon Productions films before returning one last time for the unofficial 1983 entry, 'Never Say Never Again.' 2. George Lazenby: (1969) (Image source: Reuters, YouTube/JamesBond007) Stepping into Connery's tuxedo was a tall order, and former Australian model George Lazenby only took the mission once. However, his sole outing in On Her Majesty's Secret Service gave audiences a rare glimpse of vulnerability, featuring a Bond who falls deeply in love and suffers a heartbreaking tragedy. Once overlooked, Lazenby's era is now widely praised by fans as one of the finest entries in the series. 3. Roger Moore: (1973-1985) (Image source: Reuters, YouTube/JamesBond007) Holding the record for the longest official tenure with seven films, Roger Moore steered 007 into lighter, more adventurous territory. Trading Connery's brooding edge for a raised eyebrow, a sharp quip, and outrageous gadgets, Moore kept Bond thriving through the 1970s and 80s in crowd-pleasers like 'The Spy Who Loved Me' and 'Octopussy'. 4. Timothy Dalton: (1987-1989) (Image source: Reuters, YouTube/JamesBond007) Before gritty reboots were trendy, Timothy Dalton stripped away the camp and returned to Ian Fleming’s original novels. Across 'The Living Daylights' and 'Licence to Kill', Dalton portrayed Bond as a serious, cold-blooded professional who treated espionage as a dangerous job rather than a glamorous game. Though brief, his two-film run laid the groundwork for the modern Bond we know today. 5. Pierce Brosnan: (1995-2002) (Image source: Reuters, YouTube/JamesBond007) After a six-year hiatus, Pierce Brosnan revitalised the franchise for a new generation with GoldenEye. Brosnan effortlessly blended the best of his predecessors, combining Connery’s charm, Moore’s humour, and Dalton’s intensity, while leading 007 into the blockbuster action era of the late 1990s and early 2000s. 6. Daniel Craig: (2006-2021) (Image source: Reuters, YouTube/JamesBond007) Daniel Craig shattered expectations when he took over in Casino Royale, introducing a bruised, emotionally complex, and visceral 007. For the first time, the films told a continuous, serialised story across five movies. Craig’s era broke box office records, helping push the Eon series past USD 7.8 billion worldwide (as per Deadline), and concluded with a historic, emotional farewell in No Time to Die. 7. The Next Era: Amazon MGM Studios and Robert Pattinson (Image source: Reuters, YouTube/JamesBond007) The franchise is currently undergoing its biggest behind-the-scenes transformation since 1962. Following Amazon MGM Studios taking full creative control in early 2025, with acclaimed producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman tapped to lead the charge, Robert Pattinson has been announced as the next star to inherit the 007 codename, promising a fresh, intriguing chapter for cinema's most famous spy. And speaking of what lies ahead for 007, a new creative vision and a fresh leading man are set to usher in the next chapter of the iconic franchise. James Bond proves once again that while the faces, actors and eras may change, the mission never truly ends. Robert Pattinson's first James Bond movie does not have an exact release date yet, though, as per Deadline, it is expected to release in 2028 at the earliest. Other information about the supporting cast and the title of the movie has not been revealed yet by the studio. (ANI)

item.title: West Asia conflict drives up fuel prices, inflation across ASEAN; Philippines households, businesses feel pinch

item.content:encoded:
West Asia conflict drives up fuel prices, inflation across ASEAN; Philippines households, businesses feel pinch Driven by the West Asia conflict, rising fuel and commodity prices have fuelled inflation across ASEAN, particularly in the Philippines. Surging transport and living costs are straining households, businesses, and transport workers, prompting governments to seek relief measures. ANI | Updated: 18-11-2026 14:23 IST | Created: 18-11-2026 14:23 IST

General view of the La Trinidad Vegetable Trading Post where farmers sell their produce, in La Trinidad, Benguet province, Philippines. (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

By Sahil Pandey The economic fallout of the West Asia conflict is increasingly being felt across Southeast Asia, with rising fuel prices and inflation putting pressure on households and businesses in several ASEAN countries, particularly the Philippines and Thailand. The developments have added to economic challenges across the region, with governments facing growing pressure to address rising living costs. The impact has also extended to financial markets, as currencies across major ASEAN economies have weakened against the US dollar, while stock markets in countries such as the Philippines and Malaysia have witnessed declines over the past 10-15 days. The Philippines, which relies heavily on imported fuel, has been among the countries experiencing the impact of rising energy costs, with higher transportation expenses and prices of essential commodities adding to the financial burden on ordinary citizens. The Philippines' headline inflation rate climbed to 7.8 per cent in October 2026, up from 7.2 per cent in September, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA). Transport costs recorded an annual increase of 20.1 per cent in October, compared with 14.6 per cent in the previous month, while housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuel costs rose by 9.3 per cent. The impact of rising prices is being felt across different sections of society, particularly among people dependent on daily earnings and businesses struggling to manage increasing operational expenses. Michelle, the owner of a Korean barbecue restaurant, said the sharp increase in food prices had made it increasingly difficult to manage business operations. “Actually, it’s really very difficult to manage it right now because all the prices are getting really high. And when we say high, it’s like triple high. For example, before we’re ordering our lettuce for like 70 pesos per kg. Now it’s 290,” she told ANI. She said the rising cost of ingredients had created additional challenges for restaurant owners, forcing businesses to cope with significantly higher procurement expenses. The impact is also being felt by young professionals, with rising transportation and everyday expenses adding to the financial burden on employees. Jorge Hendrick Pimentel, a 24-year-old IT professional, said inflation had affected ordinary necessities, including transportation and food, with the impact extending across different sections of society. “It has impacted everyone, especially here in IT. The impact is felt as well with regards to normal necessities like transportation, everyday survival resources like food and stuff like that,” he said. He also pointed to government initiatives, including reduced train fares and work-from-home arrangements, as measures that could help ease the burden on employees and commuters. The pressure is particularly visible among transport workers, who are directly exposed to fluctuations in fuel prices. Celso, a Filipino driver, said fuel prices had increased by nearly 50 per cent since the crisis began, significantly affecting his livelihood and adding to the financial burden on ordinary citizens. “Earlier, fuel prices were around 50 to 60 pesos per litre, but now they are averaging around 85 to 90 pesos,” he said. Highlighting the difficulties faced by lower-income households, Celso said rising fuel prices had also contributed to an increase in the cost of basic commodities, public transportation and medical services. “The low-income segment of society is the one that has really felt the impact, the squeeze. Hardly could we catch up with inflation and the daily increase in the prices of basic commodities,” he said. He added that the Philippines' heavy dependence on imported fuel had made the impact widespread, affecting people across different income groups. The pressure is also being felt in the employment sector, with businesses and employees having to adjust their financial planning to cope with rising expenses. Norlie May Maristela, who works with a hiring team, said increasing transportation costs and other living expenses had significantly affected employees' daily lives. She said businesses were also facing higher operational costs, forcing them to manage budgets and reallocate resources to deal with the changing economic situation. “Because of the increasing cost of transportation and other living expenses, it has a greater impact on our daily lives. We also have to manage our budgets and make adjustments to cope with the current situation,” Marcelino said. However, she expressed optimism over the government's efforts to address the situation, including financial assistance for affected sectors and programmes aimed at providing relief. The developments highlight the vulnerability of ASEAN economies to external energy shocks, particularly amid geopolitical tensions affecting global fuel supplies and prices. With higher energy costs feeding into transportation, food prices and business operations, the economic impact of the West Asia conflict is emerging as a key challenge for governments across Southeast Asia, which are seeking to contain inflation, protect household purchasing power and maintain economic stability. (ANI)

item.title: Operational efficiency, not price support, key to India's biogas profitability: Report
item.description: India's compressed biogas (CBG) sector is expected to improve its profitability through higher plant utilisation, assured raw material supplies and lower gas transportation costs, according to a ...
item.content:encoded:
Operational efficiency, not price support, key to India's biogas profitability: Report India's compressed biogas (CBG) sector is expected to improve its profitability through higher plant utilisation, assured raw material supplies and lower gas transportation costs, according to a report by EY-Parthenon and the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII).

ANI | Updated: 18-11-2026 13:01 IST | Created: 18-11-2026 13:01 IST

Representative image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

India's compressed biogas (CBG) sector is expected to improve its profitability through higher plant utilisation, assured raw material supplies and lower gas transportation costs, according to a report by EY-Parthenon and the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII). The report said the sector's commercial viability will increasingly depend on improving operational efficiency rather than seeking additional government price support. It noted that the focus is shifting from ensuring stable prices to improving operational and execution efficiencies. "With administered pricing providing long-term revenue visibility, the larger incremental gains are expected from interventions that improve utilisation and reduce evacuation costs," the report said. According to the report, connecting standalone CBG plants through cluster-based pipelines over the next one to three years could lower gas compression and transportation costs. It would also help ensure continuous gas evacuation and increase production. The government has approved the GOBARdhan scheme, which supports both cluster-based and standalone pipeline infrastructure to connect CBG plants with trunk pipelines and City Gas Distribution (CGD) networks. The report gave pipeline connectivity an impact score of four out of five, highlighting its potential to significantly improve project economics. It also recommended setting up biomass banks and securing long-term feedstock supply contracts over the next one to two years. These measures could help address seasonal shortages and fluctuations in raw material prices, allowing plants to operate at higher capacity. The report further suggested providing immediate relief from state Value Added Tax (VAT) on the CBG component of blended gas to reduce the tax burden and improve the economics of gas supply. It also called for fertiliser companies to increase procurement of fermented organic manure over the next one to two years. This could provide CBG producers with an additional source of revenue from by-products generated during biogas production. The report said developing a renewable gas certificate trading framework over the next two to three years or longer could create an additional revenue stream for India’s CBG producers, beyond the sale of physical biogas. It further emphasised that improving plant utilisation and reducing the cost of delivered gas would be more important for the sector's near-term commercial viability than providing additional price support. The report also highlighted India's estimated CBG production potential of 62 million metric tonnes annually. This could theoretically replace the country's projected liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports of 40 million metric tonnes and potentially save USD 20.6 billion annually. (ANI)
